body_markdown:
Hearing a pulsing or heartbeat sound in your ear at night can have simple causes, but it may sometimes be linked to pulsatile tinnitus. Learn what it means and when to speak to a doctor.


Have you ever settled into bed, rested your head on the pillow, and suddenly noticed a rhythmic thumping in your ear? It can sound surprisingly loud, almost as though your pillow has developed a heartbeat of its own.


In most cases, there is a straightforward explanation. When the surroundings become quiet at night, sounds produced inside your own body can become much easier to notice. Your position in bed can also change the way those sounds reach your ears.


However, if the sound repeatedly follows the rhythm of your heartbeat, it can sometimes be a symptom known as pulsatile tinnitus. While pulsatile tinnitus is not always a sign of something serious, persistent or unusual symptoms should be discussed with a healthcare professional.


## Why can you hear your heartbeat at night?


Your body is constantly producing sounds. Blood moves through arteries and veins, your heart pumps continuously and muscles around your head and neck are active even when you are asleep.


During the day, these internal sounds are usually masked by conversations, traffic, television, appliances and other background noise. At night, the environment is much quieter, so subtle sounds can become more noticeable.


Your sleeping position can make the effect stronger. If you sleep on your side with one ear pressed against your pillow, external sounds can become muffled. At the same time, sounds conducted through your body may seem more prominent.


This can create the strange impression that your pillow is carrying the sound of your pulse directly into your ear.


Earwax can also influence what you hear. A buildup of wax can partially block the ear canal and change the way sound is perceived. In some circumstances, this can make internal body sounds seem louder than usual.


## What is pulsatile tinnitus?


Pulsatile tinnitus is different from the more familiar form of tinnitus, which often involves ringing, buzzing, hissing or other sounds that do not follow the heartbeat.


With pulsatile tinnitus, the perceived sound has a rhythmic quality and often matches the person's pulse. Some people describe it as a whooshing, beating, thumping or pulsing noise.


It may become particularly obvious when lying down because there is less environmental noise to distract the brain. Some people notice it mainly at night, while others continue to hear it during the day.


The important point is that pulsatile tinnitus has several possible causes. Some are relatively harmless, while others involve blood vessels or changes in blood flow around the head and neck.


That does not mean that hearing a pulse in your ear automatically indicates a serious health problem. It simply means that persistent symptoms are worth investigating rather than automatically dismissing them.


## Why does lying down make it more noticeable?


Your position can affect both circulation and the way sound is transmitted around your head.


When you lie down, the relationship between your head, neck and blood vessels changes slightly. Pressing one side of your head against a pillow can also reduce outside noise and alter the acoustic environment around your ear.


There is another factor at work too: attention.


When you are trying to fall asleep, there are fewer distractions competing for your attention. Your brain can become much more aware of repetitive sounds that would normally fade into the background.


This is why a faint pulse that you barely notice during the afternoon can suddenly seem extremely loud at midnight.


## When should you be concerned?


Occasionally hearing a pulse in your ear, particularly when lying with one ear against a pillow, is not necessarily a reason for alarm.


However, it is sensible to speak with a doctor if the pulsing sound is persistent, keeps returning, becomes stronger or is present even when you are upright and moving around.


You should also mention it if the sound is noticeably different from your normal heartbeat or if it is accompanied by other symptoms.


A healthcare professional can examine your ears and ask about your symptoms. Depending on the situation, they may decide whether further assessment is appropriate.


Do not attempt to diagnose the cause yourself based solely on the sound. Pulsatile tinnitus can have different explanations, and an examination is the best way to determine whether further investigation is needed.


## Is there a simple way to test what you are hearing?


If you notice the sound at night, pay attention to its rhythm.


You can gently check your pulse at your wrist or another appropriate location and see whether the sound seems to occur at the same rate. This can provide useful information to mention to your doctor.


It is also worth noticing whether the sound changes when you sit up, turn your head or move away from the pillow.


These observations do not provide a diagnosis, but they can help you describe the experience accurately.


Avoid repeatedly poking or cleaning inside your ear in an attempt to make the sound disappear. Inserting objects into the ear can damage the ear canal or push wax deeper.


## The bottom line


Hearing a heartbeat in your ear while lying in bed can be surprisingly unsettling, but there is often a simple explanation. A quiet bedroom, your sleeping position and possible earwax buildup can make internal sounds much easier to hear.


For some people, however, a rhythmic sound that consistently matches the heartbeat may be pulsatile tinnitus. Because this type of tinnitus can sometimes be associated with vascular or other underlying conditions, persistent symptoms deserve medical attention.


The key is not to panic, but not to ignore a continuing change either. If the pulsing keeps happening, particularly if you hear it when you are away from your pillow or during the daytime, speak with a healthcare professional.


Your pillow probably does not have a heartbeat. It may simply be giving you an unusually effective way to hear your own.

If you experience persistent, worsening or unusual pulsing sounds in your ear, consult a qualified healthcare professional for an appropriate assessment.
